title: SRE SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, Reliability Initiatives, and Runbooks Ops Guidance
author: Ari Chen
body:
Summary:
This document consolidates Redwood Inference SRE standards and operational guidance for SLOs and error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review standards, operational tooling, and runbook hygiene. It is intended as the canonical reference for service owners, on-call engineers, and platform teams responsible for production reliability.

Scope and audience:
- Applies to all public-facing and internal inference services (hosted API, Dedicated control plane, Private control plane) and platform infrastructure that affect customer-facing SLOs.
- Audience: service owners, SREs, on-call engineers, product managers, and incident reviewers.

1) SLO & Error Budget Standards
Purpose: Ensure we have measurable reliability targets, actionable error budgets, and a clear process for enforcement and remediation.

SLO definition requirements:
- Each customer-facing service must have at least one latency SLO and one availability SLO.
- SLOs must be expressed in percent over a rolling 30-day window (exceptions for low-traffic services require 90-day windows; document rationale in related page).
- SLO components: objective, measurement method, data source, owner, and burn rate thresholds.

Required SLO metadata (service manifest fields):
- service_name (string)
- slo_id (string)
- slo_type (latency | availability | correctness | freshness)
- objective (e.g., "99.9% p95 latency < 120ms")
- window_days (30 | 90)
- measurement_query (promql | sql | internal_metric_name)
- owner (team alias)
- alerting_policy_id (string)

Example SLO table:
| SLO ID | Type | Objective | Window | Owner | Primary Data Source |
|---|---:|---|---:|---|---|
| api-gen-latency | latency | 99.9% p95 < 150ms | 30d | inference-team | metrics.api.p95_latency |
| api-gen-availability | availability | 99.95% success rate | 30d | inference-team | metrics.api.success_rate |

Error budget policy:
1. Define burn-rate thresholds:
   - Green: burn_rate <= 1 (no action)
   - Yellow: 1 < burn_rate <= 4 (investigate; limit non-essential releases)
   - Red: burn_rate > 4 (stop risky deploys; invoke incident review)
2. Error budget windows use the same window as the SLO (default 30d).
3. When yellow or red thresholds are crossed the SLO owner must:
   - Open an "Error Budget Action" ticket linking to the SLO and recent burn graphs.
   - Convene a 1-hour sync if status is red.
   - Document mitigations and a remediation timeline in the ticket.

Enforcement and gating:
- Releases: CI pipelines must check active error budget status for target services; red status blocks non-critical deploys in the release pipeline.
- Exec reporting: Monthly reliability dashboard must include SLO attainment and active error budget incidents.

2) Capacity Planning and Sizing
Objective: Ensure sufficient compute and accelerator capacity to meet SLOs under normal and peak workloads while optimizing cost.

Capacity planning cadence and owners:
- Quarterly capacity review led by Capacity Planning lead (eng-sre) with service owners.
- Monthly tactical reviews during peak season and before major product launches.

Required inputs for capacity model:
- Baseline QPS and 95th percentile token/sec (per-model)
- Traffic growth forecast (90/180/365 days)
- P99 latency targets and safe headroom factor (default 1.4x of observed load)
- Model performance profile (tokens/sec/GPU, memory footprint, quantization profile)
- Operational overhead: maintenance margin (default 10%), spare node pool (default 5% of pool)

Capacity calculation (summary):
1. Compute required concurrency = peak_qps * avg_tokens_per_request * avg_inflight_time (s)
2. Convert concurrency to GPU-seconds using per-model tokens/sec profile
3. Add headroom and margins
4. Map GPU-seconds to instance counts for target SKUs (e.g., A100, H100, T4)

Example capacity table (sample values):
| Service | Peak QPS | Avg tokens | p95 latency | GPUs required (A100) | Spare pool | Owner |
| inference-api | 1200 | 250 | 180ms | 18 | 2 | inference-team |
| embedding-worker | 350 | 1024 | 2s | 8 | 1 | infra-ml |

Autoscaling & bursting guidelines:
- Autoscale target: keep p95 latency below SLO under steady-state.
- Burst policies: allow 20% burst capacity for up to 10 minutes; anything longer triggers capacity review.
- Warm pools: maintain warm container/GPU warmers per model family to avoid cold-start latencies.

3) Reliability Initiatives and OKRs
Structure:
- Initiatives are tracked as 6-12 week reliability projects with a single owner and measurable success criteria (e.g., reduce p99 tail latency by 25%, increase SLO attainment to 99.95%).
- Each initiative must include: hypothesis, measurement plan (eval sets and canaries), rollout plan, rollback criteria, and post-launch review.

Typical initiative runbook:
1. Define hypothesis and metrics (owner: product + SRE).
2. Create an experiment environment and traffic mirror if needed.
3. Run pre-mortem and risk assessment.
4. Implement change behind feature flag/canary.
5. Monitor SLOs and health for 2x typical variance window.
6. Complete post-launch incident-free review.

4) Incident Review Standards (Postmortems)
Purpose: Drive blameless learning, ensure corrective actions, and close error-budget gaps.

Postmortem timeline and ownership:
- Incident ticket created at detection time with severity tagging (sev1-sev4).
- Initial triage summary within 2 hours for sev1-sev2 incidents.
- Postmortem draft submitted within 72 hours for sev1 incidents, 7 days for sev2, 14 days for sev3.
- Owner of the service is primary author; SRE helps with timeline and metric collection.

Postmortem template (required sections):
1. Summary (what happened)
2. Impact (customers, SLOs, duration)
3. Timeline (minute-level for sev1s)
4. Root cause analysis (avoid "root cause: human error" as sole explanation)
5. Contributing factors
6. Actions (short-term mitigations + long-term fixes)
7. Action owners and due dates
8. Learnings and follow-ups
9. Links to dashboards, alerts, runbooks, and commits

Action tracking and verification:
- All postmortem actions must be tracked as issues and have owners and due dates.
- Actions categorized: quick-fix (<= 7d), engineering change (<= 90d), policy/process (<= 30d).
- SRE manager verifies action completion and effectiveness (metrics) at 30d and 90d.

5) Operational Tooling and Observability Standards
Core tooling (minimum):
- Metrics backend: prometheus + long-term storage (Mimir/Thanos) for 13 months.
- Tracing: OpenTelemetry traces forwarded to our tracing backend with sampling strategy for high-volume endpoints.
- Logs: structured JSON logs indexed in central ELK/observability platform with 30d retention for standard, 365d for compliance-sensitive services.
- Error reporting: Sentry or equivalent for stack traces and exception grouping.
- Dashboards: per-service SLO dashboard (SLO attainment, burn-rate, latency percentiles, error rates).

Alerting standards:
- Alerts must map to runbooks and have documented P0/P1/P2 runbook links (attached metadata).
- Alert thresholds: prefer SLO-derived alerts (e.g., burn-rate > 1) over raw metric thresholds when possible.
- Alert noise budget: target < 1 actionable alert / engineer / on-call / day.

Operational automation:
- Alert-to-incident automation: critical alerts open incident channels and create incident tickets automatically.
- Runbook execution: support embedded runbook steps and playbook links in the incident channel (Slack).
- Chaos & periodic exercises: game-days every quarter for critical flows (routing, autoscaling, fallback).

6) SRE Runbooks Template and Examples
Runbook template (required fields):
- runbook_id
- summary
- symptoms (what the on-call will see)
- impact (who is affected)
- immediate actions (ordered checklist)
- escalation path (who to call, on-call rotation)
- mitigation steps (temporary fixes)
- recovery steps (permanent fix guidance)
- validation checks (dashboard queries, smoke tests)
- post-incident actions (create postmortem, revert changes)
- last_verified (date)

Example: High p95 latency inference-api
- symptoms: p95 latency spikes above 200ms, error rate unchanged
- immediate actions:
  1. Check SLO dashboard and burn-rate (metrics.slo.burn_rate[service])
  2. Run quick health checks: recent deploys, GC pressure, GPU memory steal, tail latencies by model id
  3. If recent deploy -> roll back to last known good revision and monitor for 15 minutes
- mitigation: scale up GPU pool by 25% (automated runbook step) and enable degraded-mode routing (route to smaller/quantized model variants)
- validation: p95 returns to below SLO for 30 minutes and burn-rate drops to green

Runbook hygiene and review:
- Every runbook must have an owner and be reviewed quarterly.
- Automated smoke tests validate core steps monthly.
- Mark runbooks with last_verified date and link to related SLO IDs.

7) Ownership, Governance, and Cadence
- SLO owners are accountable for defining SLOs, monitoring, and executing error budget policy.
- Eng-SRE is the central policy steward, responsible for running capacity cadence, maintaining templates, and verifying postmortem action completion.
- Quarterly reliability review: report (SLO attainment, active error budgets, top incident classes, capacity changes, ongoing initiatives).

8) Rollout checklist for changes that affect SLOs
1. Pre-change: update SLO/measurement if behavior changes, run risk assessment, create feature flag/canary plan.
2. Canary: deploy to 5-10% traffic with automated rollback on SLO degradation.
3. Monitor: track SLO metrics and burn-rate live for 48-72 hours.
4. Post-change: complete post-launch review and update runbooks if necessary.

- 2026-10-20: Published initial ops guidance (Ari Chen)

Notes and adoption guidance:
- Start by ensuring every service has SLO metadata and a linked runbook; use the quarterly capacity review to align owners.
- Treat the error-budget process as the primary gating mechanism for releases; it keeps short-term incentives aligned with long-term reliability.
